description:
Joey Hood, former US ambassador to Tunisia and former acting director of the Office of Iranian Affairs at the State Department, joins Al Jazeera from Washington, DC, after Iran threatened to target countries that assist US economic pressure. 

Hood says the threat should be taken seriously, pointing to Iran's recent history of striking neighbours from Pakistan to Oman, including missiles fired at the Kurdistan Regional Government's leadership just last week, alongside long-running pressure on Jordan, Syria and Lebanon through Hezbollah.

Asked whether the Strait is open, Hood says it's neither fully open nor closed: ships are getting through, some accepting real risk, while the US quietly escorts vessels through a southern corridor. He notes the UAE has doubled its tanker fleet and, per Bloomberg, is now exporting oil at pre-war levels despite Iranian threats.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Diamond Isinger, a policy strategist and former special advisor on Canada-US relations to former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, joins Al Jazeera from Vancouver to discuss the collapse of Canada-US trade talks. She says negotiations fell apart in the eleventh hour multiple times before finally breaking down, with the US bringing last-minute demands, including limits on Canada striking agreements with other international partners.

Isinger says Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliation, set to take effect September 8th, was the only realistic path forward, arguing the US administration responds best to strength. She says the move has broad, cross-partisan public support in Canada, even though it will bring short-term economic pain for both countries.

description:
Families in Gaza continue searching for children and relatives who have disappeared, with many left without answers about what happened to their loved ones. 

Nine-year-old Jalal has been missing for around three months, while Obaida, who was 15 when he disappeared at an aid distribution site, has been missing for more than a year.

Families have contacted the International Committee of the Red Cross and other international groups for information, but say they have received contradictory accounts. 

The ICRC meets families every week, helping them search for information and clarify the fate of missing people.

After years of war, tracing people is difficult. Records may have been destroyed, information is fragmented and families are often left with little more than a last known location.

Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud reports from Gaza City.

description:
Thousands of Ebola vaccine doses have arrived in the Democratic Republic of Congo as health authorities step up efforts to contain the country’s worst-ever outbreak.

The doses come from the global stockpile of Ervebo vaccines, which were developed for previous Ebola responses. The vaccine has not been cleared for the Bundibugyo strain behind the current outbreak, but the World Health Organization says early data suggests it may offer some protection, with more research needed.

More than 2,500 people have died in the outbreak, with the United Nations warning that the epidemic is growing rapidly and spreading across a vast area.

In Beni, near the epicentre, local groups are working to raise awareness and encourage communities to take the outbreak seriously. Response efforts have also been hampered by attacks on health workers and ongoing violence between government forces and armed groups.

Al Jazeera’s Kelvin Kimathi reports.

The two economies are deeply linked, with roughly $880 billion in goods and services traded last year. About 72 percent of Canada’s merchandise exports go to the US.

The tariffs could raise prices for US consumers and put pressure on Canadian producers as businesses absorb higher costs or face reduced demand. The impact could also extend to energy, manufacturing and other industries that depend on access to the US market.

If trade slows, companies could cut production, postpone investment or reduce hiring, putting jobs at risk.

description:
Heat stress is rising worldwide as human-induced climate change makes extremely high temperatures more frequent and severe, and Japan is adapting to a new reality of dangerous summer heat. At one flower farm, workers now harvest at night under greenhouse lights after a colleague suffered heatstroke. In a single week last month, more than 10,800 people were treated for heatstroke, double the number from the same period in 2025. In Osaka, warehouse worker Taichi Konishi cools down by stepping into what's effectively a human refrigerator: "It feels really good. I only went in for about two minutes, but even that was enough for all my sweat to dry up." 

Cara Legg reports for Al Jazeera.

On China, described as Iran's biggest potential economic lifeline, Harrison says the real question isn't whether Washington can police compliance but whether it's willing to risk damaging US-China relations, especially with a Trump-Xi summit looming next month.
